posts.dek: Pull up a chair. The field is fixed, Game 1 tips Sunday and every series has a reason to keep a second screen open.

sections.title: The opening whistle: Minnesota (1) vs. New York (8)
paragraphs: Sunday, Sept. 27 · 2 p.m. ET · ABC. The Lynx earned the top seed; the Liberty get the hardest possible road from the eighth spot. Can New York find enough creation to make the favorite uncomfortable?

sections.title: The new guard: Golden State (2) vs. Dallas (7)
paragraphs: Sunday, Sept. 27 · 4 p.m. ET · ABC. Golden State made an expansion season look like an instant contender. Dallas brings Paige Bueckers and a dangerous offense. Watch which bench survives a shorter postseason rotation.

sections.title: The star test: Las Vegas (3) vs. Indiana (6)
paragraphs: Sunday, Sept. 27 · time to be confirmed · Prime Video. A’ja Wilson anchors the Aces; Indiana arrives with Caitlin Clark and Kelsey Mitchell. Check the live schedule for the tip time before making plans.

sections.title: The late window: Atlanta (4) vs. Washington (5)
paragraphs: Sunday, Sept. 27 · 9 p.m. ET · USA. Atlanta has home court, and Washington has already proved it can disrupt higher seeds. Watch for the possession-by-possession swing.

sections.title: Keep the bracket in pencil
paragraphs: The first round is best of three, with a 1–1–1 home format. The semifinals are best of five; the Finals are best of seven. Follow the live game board for scores and schedule updates.

posts.seriesLabel: FOOD FOR THOUGHT · CONNECTICUT SUN FAREWELL
posts.title: One Last Sunrise: Farewell to the Connecticut Sun
posts.imageAlt: Connecticut Sun fans celebrate the franchise at its final home game in Mohegan Sun Arena
posts.dek: The final record was 11–33. The final result was a win. Between those two facts sits 24 seasons of Connecticut basketball that deserve to be remembered.

sections.title: A final night worth keeping
paragraphs: Connecticut beat Toronto 95–81 at Mohegan Sun Arena on Sept. 24, 2026. The Sun ended their last season 11–33, with a one-game winning streak. A hard year did not get the last word: the players and crowd got one more win together.
The team is moving to Houston and will be renamed the Comets in 2027. Connecticut fans have every right to hold on to what was built in Uncasville.

sections.title: 2003: a home by the river
paragraphs: After the Orlando Miracle relocated, the Mohegan Tribe brought the franchise to Connecticut in 2003. Playing at Mohegan Sun Arena made the Sun a place people traveled to, returned to and claimed as their own. The Tribe’s ownership was a defining part of the identity.

sections.title: 2004 and 2005: the first close calls
paragraphs: Mike Thibault’s early Sun reached back-to-back WNBA Finals. Seattle won in 2004; Sacramento won in 2005. Lindsay Whalen, Nykesha Sales and Asjha Jones helped set a standard: Connecticut could meet the league’s best on the biggest stage.

sections.title: 2019 and 2022: the door stayed open
paragraphs: The 2019 Sun took Washington to a deciding fifth game in the Finals. In 2022, behind a bruising frontcourt featuring Alyssa Thomas, DeWanna Bonner, Brionna Jones and Jonquel Jones, Connecticut made its fourth Finals appearance. Different faces, familiar promise: the Sun were never easy to put away.

sections.title: The people who gave the jersey its weight
paragraphs: Jonquel Jones won the 2021 MVP award as a Sun and had her No. 35 honored at the arena in 2026. Alyssa Thomas turned versatility and toughness into a team language. Across eras, players, coaches, staff and supporters made Connecticut a fixture in the postseason conversation.
No championship banner arrived. Four Finals trips did, and so did the habit of believing the next one could be different. That is a legacy bigger than one difficult final standings line.

sections.title: One game, one streak, decades of light
paragraphs: The final box score reads Sun 95, Tempo 81. It cannot show every seat filled across 24 seasons, or every player who grew into herself in this building. The name leaves the schedule. The memories, and the people who made them, stay in Connecticut.

posts.seriesLabel: FOOD FOR THOUGHT · PLAYOFF BENCH TEST
posts.title: The Fever Got the Bench. What Did Minnesota Actually Give Away?
posts.imageAlt: Official WNBA headshot of Indiana Fever guard Caitlin Clark
posts.storyImageCaption: Indiana beat Minnesota 96-77 on Sept. 22. Image: official WNBA player media.
posts.dek: Indiana needed the win. Minnesota needed to get healthy. By halftime, those priorities were obvious. The Fever took the 96-77 win, but the second half became something else: a live playoff-depth test.

rankings.note: The deepest playoff bench by a mile. Janelle Salaun is a Sixth Player favorite, Tiffany Hayes brings another veteran creator, and Golden State can change lineups without changing its identity.
Marine Johannes gives New York instant offense and movement. The Liberty second unit is efficient enough to survive short starter rests without asking one player to do everything.
Dallas gets useful scoring and activity from its reserves. The question is how much of that survives when playoff rotations shrink.
Jewell Loyd gives Vegas something most benches do not have: a former All-Star who can still take over possessions. The Aces do not need huge bench minutes, just dependable ones.
Sophie Cunningham keeps pace and spacing around the stars. Indiana's bench is not the headline, but it can keep the offense from falling off a cliff.
Young, physical and willing to defend. Washington's depth matters because the Mystics can keep size on the floor when the starters sit.
Atlanta leans harder on its starting group. The bench has been efficient, but the playoff question is whether it can buy enough clean minutes for the stars.
Lowest regular-season bench scoring among the playoff field, but Tuesday showed why raw bench PPG can lie. Minnesota's reserves cut a 29-point hole to eight before Indiana's starters closed it out.

rows: 12.9 PPG, 39.7% from three, league-leading 492 bench points
Primary second-unit scorer and a real late-game option
8.7 PPG with playmaking and movement shooting
Change the geometry of the floor when New York gets sticky
8.3 PPG in bench games, 43%+ from three
Keep pace, spacing and edge around Clark and Mitchell
Veteran shot creation from the second unit
Give Vegas a scorer who does not need the starters to create her look

sections.title: Did Minnesota prioritize rest?
paragraphs: Not from the opening tip. Olivia Miles was already out with a calf injury, but Minnesota started Napheesa Collier, Kayla McBride, Courtney Williams and the rest of its available first unit. Indiana then punched them in the mouth. The Fever led 31-16 after one quarter and pushed the margin to 29 in the first half.

That is when Cheryl Reeve changed the assignment. She sat her starters for most of the final two and a half quarters because she did not want to risk another injury. So yes, rest and health became the priority, but only after Indiana had already taken control. Calling the entire win gift wrapped lets Minnesota's starters off too easily.

sections.title: Still, Indiana got a very nice gift
paragraphs: Indiana needed this one to keep its home-court hopes alive. Instead of spending 40 minutes dealing with Minnesota's best five, the Fever spent most of the second half playing the Lynx reserves.

The funny part is that the bench made Indiana work. Chloe Bibby hit five threes and scored 15. Liatu King had 12 points, four rebounds and three steals. Aari McDonald added 10 points and five assists. Minnesota cut a 29-point deficit to eight before Caitlin Clark, Kelsey Mitchell and Aliyah Boston finally shut the door.

sections.title: That is the part Minnesota should keep
paragraphs: The loss matters because the No. 1 seed still is not clinched. The way the bench responded matters for a different reason. Playoff benches are not supposed to win four-minute stretches by accident. They have to survive foul trouble, injuries and the ugly minutes when a starter needs air.

Minnesota ranks last among the eight playoff teams in regular-season bench scoring. Tuesday did not magically make the Lynx the deepest team in the field. It did show that their reserves can defend, run and drag a game back into range when the stars are sitting.

sections.title: Golden State has the bench everybody else has to answer
paragraphs: Golden State is in its own category. The Valkyries are around 36 bench points per game, roughly 13 more than the next playoff team. Janelle Salaun has 492 points off the bench, the most in the league, while shooting 39.7 percent from three.

That depth already mattered after Berlin. With several World Cup players resting, Golden State still beat Portland 82-66 behind Laeticia Amihere and Kaitlyn Chen. That is not emergency depth. That is part of the system.

sections.title: The Sixth Woman board
paragraphs: Salaun is the standard here. ESPN's four-person awards panel unanimously picked her for Sixth Player of the Year, and the production backs up the attention. Marine Johannes gives New York a different kind of weapon, Sophie Cunningham keeps Indiana's second unit connected to its spacing, and Jewell Loyd gives Las Vegas a scorer with starter-level experience.

The playoffs will shrink rotations, but that makes these players more important, not less. The question is not who has ten playable bodies. It is who has a sixth and seventh player a coach actually trusts when the game gets tight.

sections.title: Shak's read
paragraphs: Indiana earned the lead. Minnesota chose not to chase it with its starters. Both things can be true.

The Fever got exactly what they needed: a win without having to beat Minnesota's best lineup for four quarters. The Lynx got something too: a long look at the players who may have to save a playoff possession, a quarter or a game when the plan goes sideways.
Thursday's rematch is the one that tells us more. If Minnesota brings the full group and treats it like a playoff tune-up, then we finally get the matchup Tuesday was supposed to be.

debates: Did Minnesota make the right call pulling the starters?
Which playoff bench do you trust most for a seven-minute stretch?
Would you rather have one elite sixth woman or three dependable reserves?

posts.title: The Seats Are Moving
posts.dek: Everybody already has a playoff ticket. Now the seats are moving. Atlanta took another step toward home court, New York is officially opening on the road, and Dallas finally got clipped after six straight wins.

sections.title: Atlanta keeps handling business
paragraphs: Atlanta came back from Berlin and apparently decided losing could wait. The Dream beat New York 95-84 on Monday and moved to 29-14.
That makes three straight wins since the break. One more win over New York on Wednesday, or one Indiana loss, locks up first-round home court for Atlanta.

sections.title: New York, pack a road bag
paragraphs: The Liberty had a nice little run going. They beat Minnesota, put 106 on Toronto and came home with a chance to keep pushing up the bracket.
Atlanta ended that. New York is 26-17 now, and first-round home court is officially gone. The Liberty are in. They are just starting the playoffs in somebody else's building.

sections.title: Dallas finally blinked
paragraphs: Dallas won six straight and made the bottom of the bracket a whole lot more interesting. Then Phoenix stole one by a point.
Kahleah Copper's layup with two seconds left gave the Mercury an 87-86 win. Paige Bueckers had 30 points and seven assists, but the last shot did not fall. Dallas is 26-17 with one game left.

sections.title: Shak's bite
paragraphs: Everybody has a ticket. Nobody has the same seat they thought they had a few days ago.

Atlanta is trying to keep home court. New York knows it is traveling. Dallas just lost its six-game heater. Minnesota still has Golden State behind it, and Vegas is sitting right in the middle of the top-four mess.
Two days left. Keep the bracket in pencil.

posts.title: The Playoff Trio Test: Who Scores, Who Stops, and Who Matches Their Seed?
posts.week: Playoff field set · stats through Sept. 20
posts.imageAlt: Washington Mystics players attack the basket against the Indiana Fever in an official WNBA game photo
posts.storyImageCaption: Washington's young core helped the Mystics beat Indiana 93-77 on Sept. 20. Official WNBA photography via the Washington Mystics.
posts.dek: The top eight stayed in the same order after the FIBA break, but they did not come back looking the same. Here is the trio each playoff team trusts to create points, erase them, or do a little of both.

trioDashboard.title: Three players. Two sides of the ball. Eight very different playoff plans.
trioDashboard.intro: Switch the board between scoring production, defensive context, and the first two games after the FIBA break. The seed on each card stays put so you can see where the numbers agree with the standings and where they start an argument.
trioDashboard.methodology: Production is ranked by the trio's combined 2026 points per game, with assists and team offensive rating shown for context. Limiting scoring is ranked by team defensive rating because defense belongs to all five players; trio steals and blocks show activity without pretending they tell the whole story. Post-FIBA form covers two games per team. It is a temperature check, not a season-sized conclusion.

teams.offenseNote: Miles, Collier, and McBride all score at least 17.9 per game. Miles supplies the table setting while McBride stretches the floor.
teams.defenseNote: Collier and Miles give Minnesota length at the point of attack, while McBride keeps pressure on the ball. The trio averages 6.2 steals plus blocks.
teams.breakNote: The trio held near its season scoring level at 54.0 points per game, but Minnesota split its two games and saw its lead over Golden State shrink to one game.

teams.offenseNote: This is not Golden State's top scoring trio. It is the trio that defines how the Valkyries win. Salaün, Hayes, and Chen supply more of the points.
teams.defenseNote: No playoff team allows fewer points per 100 possessions. Burton crowds the ball, Williams blows up actions, and Stokes protects the rim.
teams.breakNote: Golden State allowed only 61.5 points per game while Gabby Williams sat out both games after her World Cup run. That is equal parts impressive and mildly terrifying.

teams.identity: The league's most trusted closing trio
teams.offenseNote: Wilson bends the defense, Young punishes the second read, and Gray still knows exactly which button to push late. Their 16.5 assists matter as much as the scoring.
teams.defenseNote: The team defense ranks fifth in this field, but Wilson gives every coverage a reset button. Young can take the most difficult perimeter assignment.
teams.breakNote: The trio jumped from 57.5 season points per game to 68.5 after the break. Wilson averaged 29.5 and Young averaged 29.0. FIBA did not cool them off.

teams.identity: The cleanest two-way trio in the field
teams.offenseNote: Gray and Howard stretch the floor while Reese creates paint pressure and extra possessions. None of the three has to win the same way.
teams.defenseNote: Their 7.5 steals plus blocks lead every trio on this board. Howard creates chaos, Gray stays attached, and Reese closes the possession on the glass.
teams.breakNote: Atlanta posted the best return-week margin at plus 34.5. Reese averaged 26.5 points, while Howard moved the ball and the trio combined for 8.5 steals plus blocks per game.

teams.identity: The loudest offense and the biggest swing
teams.offenseNote: No trio in the field scores more. Mitchell's efficiency, Clark's range and passing, and Boston's interior touch force opponents to guard the whole floor.
teams.defenseNote: Indiana ranks last among playoff teams in defensive rating. Boston can cover mistakes, but she should not have to clean up every leak by herself.
teams.breakNote: The trio still averaged 61.5 points after the break, but Indiana split the games and Boston fell to 7.5 points per game. The triangle works best when the paint gets fed too.

teams.identity: A lower seed with championship muscle memory
teams.offenseNote: The season numbers are quieter than the names. Stewart remains the pressure point, Jones owns the glass, and Ionescu can turn one paint touch into a three-point avalanche.
teams.defenseNote: The rating says seventh in this field. The post-break activity says pay attention: the trio produced 8.0 steals plus blocks per game in two wins.
teams.breakNote: New York beat first-place Minnesota and then scored 106 in Toronto. Stewart averaged 25.5 points, while Ionescu shifted toward creation at 7.5 assists per game.

teams.identity: Young size that already plays grown-up defense
teams.offenseNote: Austin and Iriafen punish the glass, while Citron keeps the floor connected. Their combined 22.7 rebounds lead every trio on the board.
teams.defenseNote: Washington ranks third in this playoff field on defense. Size, rebounding, and Citron's positional discipline let the Mystics finish possessions instead of defending twice.
teams.breakNote: Washington returned 2-0 even though Citron missed the first game. Against Indiana, Iriafen and Austin both went for 20-point double-doubles and Citron added nine assists.

teams.identity: Three creators hiding behind the eighth seed
teams.offenseNote: Bueckers and Ogunbowale draw the eyes, but Shepard is the hinge. Her scoring, rebounding, and passing keep Dallas from becoming a turn-taking offense.
teams.defenseNote: The trio does not create many steals or blocks, yet Dallas sits sixth in this field defensively. The challenge is getting stops without losing its best offensive spacing.
teams.breakNote: The Wings came back 2-0 and this trio averaged 17.5 assists. Shepard supplied 8.5 of them, giving Dallas another way to organize when the guards get crowded.

sections.title: The standings stayed still. The pressure did not.
paragraphs: Every playoff team returned from the World Cup break in the same seed it holds now. Minnesota remained first. Golden State remained second. Las Vegas, Atlanta, and Indiana held the middle. New York, Washington, and Dallas stayed tied at 26 wins, with the official tiebreak order placing them sixth, seventh, and eighth.

That sounds calm until you look at the scores. Every playoff team returned at .500 or better, and six won both games. Atlanta outscored opponents by 34.5 points per game, Las Vegas by 29.0, New York by 24.5, and Washington by 23.0. The chairs did not move, but several teams came back trying to flip the table.

sections.title: Minnesota has the best seed, not the loudest trio.
paragraphs: Olivia Miles, Napheesa Collier, and Kayla McBride rank third in combined scoring and fourth in team defensive context. That balance helps explain why Minnesota still owns the league's best record. There is no single coverage that solves all three: Miles can get downhill or create, McBride punishes help, and Collier connects both ends.

The catch is continuity. Collier has played only 14 games, so the Lynx have spent most of the year building first-place habits without a full season from one of their best players. The first two games back produced a flat zero scoring margin. Minnesota is still the standard, but the cushion is gone.

sections.title: Golden State is the only team whose trio starts with a stop.
paragraphs: Gabby Williams, Veronica Burton, and Kiah Stokes rank last in combined scoring on this board because that is not their assignment. Their job is to make the opponent's first option uncomfortable, the second option late, and the third option somebody the scouting report was willing to live with.

Golden State owns the best defensive rating in the field and held Portland and Seattle to 61.5 points per game after the break. Williams did not play in either game. If she returns ready, the second seed may add its most disruptive defender to a group that just went 2-0 without her.

sections.title: Las Vegas has the trio nobody wants to see in the last five minutes.
paragraphs: A'ja Wilson, Jackie Young, and Chelsea Gray combine for 57.5 points and 16.5 assists per game. Wilson can finish the possession, Young can win the advantage, and Gray can decide which matchup gets tested until it breaks. Their second-place production rank undersells how well the three jobs fit together.

The return was loud. Wilson averaged 29.5 points, Young averaged 29.0, and the trio reached 68.5 points per game as Las Vegas went 2-0 with a plus 29.0 margin. That is not a warm-up. That is a warning label.

sections.title: Atlanta owns the most complete trio on the board.
paragraphs: Allisha Gray, Rhyne Howard, and Angel Reese are fourth in scoring and second in team defense. They also lead every trio here with 7.5 combined steals and blocks per game. Gray and Howard make the floor wide. Reese makes the possession longer. All three can turn defense into points before the opponent gets set.

Atlanta's post-break trio scoring dipped slightly, but the team won by 34.5 points per game. Reese averaged 26.5 points, Howard created 6.0 assists per game, and the trio averaged 8.5 steals plus blocks. That is the difference between three stars sharing a court and three players multiplying one another.

sections.title: Indiana can win a shootout. The playoffs will ask for another answer.
paragraphs: Kelsey Mitchell, Caitlin Clark, and Aliyah Boston are the clear production champions at 64.2 combined points per game. Indiana also owns the best team offensive rating in the league. Mitchell's efficiency, Clark's passing range, and Boston's interior skill can make a defense pick the least comfortable way to lose.

The other side is the issue. Indiana ranks eighth among these teams in defensive rating and returned with a 1-1 record and a plus 1.0 margin. Boston averaged only 7.5 points in those two games. If the Fever become too perimeter-heavy, a great trio turns into two scorers and a cleanup crew.

sections.title: New York is playing better than sixth place sounds.
paragraphs: Breanna Stewart, Sabrina Ionescu, and Jonquel Jones rank sixth in scoring and seventh in team defense, which lines up neatly with New York's seed. The last two games did not look neat at all. The Liberty beat first-place Minnesota, scored 106 in Toronto, and posted a plus 24.5 margin.

Stewart came back from a World Cup MVP run averaging 25.5 points. Ionescu shifted toward playmaking at 7.5 assists, and the trio averaged 8.0 steals plus blocks. New York may still be sixth in the standings, but it no longer looks like the sixth-most dangerous team.

sections.title: Washington is the seed nobody should read too quickly.
paragraphs: Shakira Austin, Sonia Citron, and Kiki Iriafen rank seventh in trio scoring, but third in team defense and first in combined rebounding at 22.7 per game. Their production is not built on one guard carrying every late clock. It is built on size, patience, paint touches, and finishing the defensive possession.

The Mystics returned 2-0 even with Citron missing the first game. Against Indiana, Iriafen and Austin both recorded 20-point double-doubles, while Citron added 16 points and nine assists. Seventh seed, yes. Seventh-best trio, no.

sections.title: Dallas has three creators, not two stars and a helper.
paragraphs: Paige Bueckers and Arike Ogunbowale are the obvious pressure points. Jessica Shepard is what changes the geometry. She averages 14.3 points, 10.9 rebounds, and 5.1 assists, which gives Dallas a frontcourt organizer when guards are blitzed or denied.

The trio averaged 17.5 assists after the break and Dallas won both games. The Wings still rank only sixth among playoff teams on defense, so their path is narrow: keep the ball moving, avoid empty possessions, and make the opponent guard all three creators on the same trip.

sections.title: Shak's call: the best trio depends on the question.
paragraphs: Need the most points? Indiana. Need one closing possession? Las Vegas. Need to drag a game into the mud? Golden State. Need the cleanest two-way blend? Atlanta. Need a lower seed capable of wrecking the bracket? Washington and New York are standing right there.

The standings reward the full season, and they should. A playoff series is a different exam. It asks whether your three most important players can keep solving the same opponent after the easy answers are gone. Atlanta has the fewest obvious weak spots. Las Vegas has the most trustworthy closer. Indiana has the highest offensive ceiling. That is why the field is settled and the argument is just getting started.

debates: Would you rather enter a playoff series with Indiana's first-ranked trio offense or Golden State's first-ranked defense?
Is Atlanta's two-way balance more valuable than Las Vegas having the best closer in A'ja Wilson?
Which tied 26-16 team is most dangerous: New York, Washington, or Dallas?
Does Minnesota's balance still make the Lynx the favorite after a 1-1 return from the break?

foodSegment.title: A Big Three Is a Job Description
foodSegment.script: Three famous names do not automatically make a playoff trio. Somebody has to create the advantage. Somebody has to finish it. Somebody has to stop the other team from doing the same thing. Indiana brings the biggest plate of points. Golden State takes the plate away. Atlanta might be the one team that can do both before you sit down.

posts.seriesLabel: SNACK SHAK BYTE · USA WHEELCHAIR BASKETBALL
posts.title: One Free Throw, Sixteen Years, and Gold: USA Is Back on Top
posts.dek: Canada tied it with 39.1 seconds left. Courtney Ryan hit the free throw that made it 77–76. Twenty seconds later, Team USA had its first women’s wheelchair basketball world title since 2010 and a new runway toward LA 2028.

sections.title: The last point became the whole story
paragraphs: A championship game can hold an entire sixteen-year wait inside one free throw. Host Canada pulled even at 76 with 39.1 seconds left in Ottawa. Courtney Ryan went to the line with 20.8 seconds remaining, missed the first and made the second. That was the final point of the 2026 women’s world championship.

Lindsey Zurbrugg led the United States with 26 points. Rose Hollermann and Ryan scored 17 each, and Ryan finished one rebound and one assist shy of a triple-double with nine assists and eight boards. Canada still had chances after the go-ahead free throw, but the U.S. defense survived the final possessions and the horn made 77–76 official.

sections.title: Sixteen years between world titles
paragraphs: The United States won the first women’s wheelchair basketball World Championship in 1990 and its second in 2010. Ottawa makes three. The gap matters because this was not a program strolling back into a familiar seat. The Netherlands had won the previous two world titles, and the U.S. had not even reached a world final since 2010.
That history made the last minute feel heavier. Team USA did not need a comfortable ending. It needed one more point, one more stop and one more possession that did not belong to Canada.

sections.title: Now LA 2028 looks different
paragraphs: The U.S. women won Paralympic silver in Paris in 2024 after bronze in Tokyo. Now the same broader program enters the next Paralympic cycle as the reigning world champion. Eleven of the twelve players on the Ottawa roster had previous Paralympic wheelchair basketball experience, while 18-year-old Arelle Middleton brought Paralympic experience from track and field.

A home Paralympics is still two years away, which is forever in roster time. But world gold changes the starting point. Team USA is no longer chasing proof that it can get back to the top. Ottawa just supplied the receipt.

debates: Does the 2026 world title change how you view Team USA heading toward LA 2028?
Who was the championship-game difference maker: Zurbrugg’s 26 points, Ryan’s all-around line or the final defensive stand?
What part of the veteran core should Team USA protect most as the roster evolves?

foodSegment.title: Shak’s bite: one point, sixteen years
foodSegment.script: Canada erased the lead. The building was ready for one more swing. Courtney Ryan made one free throw, the U.S. got the stop, and sixteen years disappeared at the horn. World champions again. Sometimes the whole meal is one point.

posts.title: The Race Is Real. The Trophy Is A’ja’s to Lose.
posts.imageAlt: Official WNBA headshot of Las Vegas Aces center A’ja Wilson
posts.storyImageCaption: A’ja Wilson enters the final week at the top of the official WNBA MVP analysis and the current MVP betting market.
posts.dek: Five candidates, five different definitions of value. The live case board tests scoring, playmaking, efficiency, team context and published on/off impact — and the most complete argument still points to A’ja Wilson.

sections.title: The case in one number
paragraphs: Las Vegas has a +12.1 net rating with Wilson on the court and -14.2 with her off in the WNBA’s September 17 MVP analysis. That 26.3-point swing is the center of the argument: the Aces become a fundamentally different team when No. 22 sits.

sections.title: The race got louder
paragraphs: Kelsey Mitchell broke Wilson’s single-season points record on September 18 and reached 1,034 points. Olivia Miles remains the engine of the league-leading Lynx, Caitlin Clark owns the strongest pure playmaking case in the group, and Paige Bueckers continues to pair efficient scoring with high-level creation for playoff-bound Dallas.

sections.title: Why it is still A’ja’s to lose
paragraphs: Wilson leads the league in scoring average and blocks, carries the league’s highest usage rate in the WNBA’s latest MVP analysis, anchors a top-three team and owns the strongest published two-way impact profile among the leading candidates. There are better counterarguments now. There is not yet a better complete argument.

debates: Should total points matter more than scoring average when Kelsey Mitchell now owns the single-season record?
How much extra MVP weight should Olivia Miles receive for driving the No. 1 team as a rookie?
Does Indiana having two legitimate MVP candidates strengthen the Fever’s case or split it?

posts.title: Berlin to Buckets: The Playoff Teams Came Back Loud
posts.week: September 17 return night · Updated after Sept. 18 playoff ripple
posts.imageAlt: Las Vegas Aces and Seattle Storm in action on September 17, 2026
posts.storyImageCaption: Las Vegas faced Seattle on WNBA return night. Photo: Scott Eklund, NBAE, via the Las Vegas Aces.
posts.dek: Return night opened with four playoff teams going 4–0 by a combined +131. One night later, New York beat No. 1 Minnesota, Indiana stayed tied with Atlanta in the top-four fight, and Golden State clinched first-round home court while moving within one game of the top seed.

sections.title: Return night in one number
paragraphs: The four playoff teams in action on September 17 combined for a +131 scoring margin. Atlanta won by 44, Washington by 30, Dallas by 20 and Las Vegas by 37.

sections.title: Friday changed the bracket math
paragraphs: New York beat Minnesota 93–81 to move to 25–16 and sixth in the current playoff order. Minnesota fell to 31–10 and has lost three straight.

Golden State beat Portland 82–66, improved to 30–11, clinched first-round home court and moved within one game of Minnesota for the No. 1 seed. Indiana also improved to 27–14 with a 103–85 win over Toronto, keeping the No. 4 race with Atlanta alive.

sections.title: Why it matters
paragraphs: The return from Berlin is no longer a one-night story. Contenders are converting international momentum, depth and rest into meaningful seeding pressure, and the standalone feature now tracks both the original +131 return night and the next-day playoff ripple.

posts.title: Seven Passports, One Playbook: Are the Liberty the Post FIBA Finals Sleeper?
posts.week: Post World Cup reset · Updated after NYL 93, MIN 81
posts.imageAlt: Liberty players Pauline Astier, Marine Johannes, Breanna Stewart, Leonie Fiebich and Raquel Carrera in a national team composite
posts.storyImageCaption: Five Liberty players reached the World Cup semifinals: Pauline Astier and Marine Johannes with France, Breanna Stewart with USA, Leonie Fiebich with Germany and Raquel Carrera with Spain. Graphic supplied by Shak, via ClutchPoints.
posts.dek: New York sent a league-high seven players to the World Cup, then came out of the break and beat No. 1 Minnesota 93–81 on the road. The Liberty are 25–16 and sixth in the current playoff order. The sleeper question just got its first receipt.

rows: The closer is already in championship rhythm.
14.0 PPG, a tournament-high 20 threes and silver
New York needs her range and imagination, not just spot-up minutes.
A second organizer can keep the offense alive when pressure rises.
9.9 PPG, 8.6 RPG, 3.6 APG and All-Star Five
Size, rebounding and connective passing travel in any lineup.
A physical frontcourt option when playoff matchups get heavy.
A matchup breaker, if New York makes room for meaningful minutes.
9.0 PPG, 2.7 RPG and 2.0 steals plus blocks per game
Length and activity deepen a defense that may need new answers.

sections.title: This is what a sleeper looks like
paragraphs: A team with Breanna Stewart, Sabrina Ionescu and Jonquel Jones should not be able to sneak up on anybody. Yet New York reached the World Cup break at 24 wins and 16 losses, sitting sixth in a crowded playoff race. That seed has become camouflage for a roster with much more championship equity than its place in the standings suggests.

No WNBA team sent more players to Berlin. Seven Liberty players represented six countries, and New York had at least one player on each of the four semifinal teams. They did not simply collect passport stamps. They carried offenses, cleaned the glass, created shots and made medal-winning decisions.

sections.title: The World Cup changed the question
paragraphs: Stewart returned with gold, a second World Cup MVP award and a 22-point, 10-rebound performance in the final. Marine Johannes returned with silver after leading the tournament with 20 made threes. Leonie Fiebich became the first German player named to a Women's World Cup All-Star Five. Han Xu averaged 18.8 points and 10.8 rebounds. Raquel Carrera helped Spain win bronze, while Pauline Astier and Elizabeth Balogun showed they can make winning plays beyond the roles New York usually gives them.

So the question is no longer whether the Liberty have enough talent. Berlin settled that rather loudly. The question is whether New York can bring those fuller versions of its players back into one system without asking everybody to shrink again.

sections.title: The first post-break receipt came in Minnesota
paragraphs: The theory got a real test immediately. New York went to Minnesota and beat the top-seeded Lynx 93–81 despite having seven players return from the World Cup. Breanna Stewart led the way with 24 points and 10 rebounds, Sabrina Ionescu added 17 points and six assists, Pauline Astier scored 14, and Marine Johannès added 13 off the bench.

That matters because the concern was never whether New York had enough individual talent. It was whether the international versions of these players could come back without shrinking into narrower club roles. Against Minnesota, the Liberty got creation, shooting and closing contributions from several places. They moved to 25–16 and sixth in the current playoff order while handing Minnesota a third straight loss.

sections.title: Can seven international weapons fit one playoff rotation?
paragraphs: They can, but being dynamic together does not mean everybody needs more shots. It means more ways to start and finish a possession. Let Johannes bend the floor instead of parking her in the corner. Use Fiebich as a rebounder and connector. Let Han punish smaller lineups. Trust Astier to organize a second unit. Keep Stewart moving through actions instead of making every important possession a rescue mission.

There is another advantage hiding in plain sight. While seven teammates competed in Berlin, Ionescu, Jones, Rebekah Gardner and the rest of New York's stay-home group had time to recover. The Liberty are not returning as one tired team. They are combining a rested core with an internationally sharpened one. That can be powerful, if the handoff is clean.

sections.title: The case against the sleeper pick
paragraphs: A sixth seed still has to win difficult games away from home. The World Cup players also return with travel in their legs, different terminology in their heads and very little time to rebuild WNBA timing. International confidence can travel overnight. Chemistry usually prefers a connecting flight.

Role compression is the larger danger. If New York returns to predictable possessions, watches Stewart and Ionescu create everything, and treats the international breakout performances as souvenirs, the roster will look deep without playing deep. The postseason will punish that gap quickly.

sections.title: Shak's call: 8.2 out of 10 sleeper heat
paragraphs: Yes, the Liberty are a real Finals sleeper. They are not the favorite, and the sixth seed is not an accident, but few lower-seeded teams can change style this many ways. New York can play through elite stars, size, shooting, switching, secondary creation or a giant at center. Most opponents can solve one version. A connected Liberty team can keep changing the exam.
The world just watched seven Liberty players become more of themselves. If New York lets them stay that way together, sixth place may become the most misleading number in the bracket.

debates: Should New York expand Han Xu's playoff role after her 18.8-point, 10.8-rebound World Cup?
Can the Liberty preserve Marine Johannes' freedom when the offense returns to its usual hierarchy?
Does international success make New York the most dangerous lower seed in the field?

posts.title: Gold Is Earned Twice: What USA Got Right Against France
posts.imageAlt: Team USA celebrating the 2026 FIBA Women's Basketball World Cup championship in Berlin
posts.dek: France won the opening argument. Team USA won the adjustment. The scoring, rebounding, momentum and player dashboards explain how a 14-point hole became a 97-79 championship victory.

sections.title: The championship hinge
paragraphs: France built a 14-point lead behind a 21-2 run, but USA cut the deficit to two at halftime and won the third quarter 30-12. The comeback was a sequence of veteran decisions, defensive adjustments and extra chances on the glass.

sections.title: The final read
paragraphs: France proved USA can be moved. USA proved that moving a champion and finishing one are still two different assignments.

debates: Which USA adjustment changed the final most?

posts.title: Jackie Young Has Completed the Championship Collection
posts.imageAlt: Jackie Young smiling with her gold medal, draped in the American flag and holding two championship trophies
posts.storyImageCaption: Jackie Young celebrates World Cup gold after helping USA defeat France 97-79 in Berlin.
posts.dek: High school. NCAA. Three WNBA titles. Olympic gold in 3x3 and 5x5. Now Jackie Young can add FIBA World Cup champion to a résumé that has won everywhere.

sections.title: The final box is checked
paragraphs: Some players chase one championship. Jackie Young apparently prefers the full set. Young added FIBA Women's Basketball World Cup gold after helping Team USA overcome a 14-point deficit and defeat France 97-79 in Berlin. She delivered 18 points and five assists, including a crucial third-quarter three that helped the United States take control.

The victory fills one of the few remaining spaces in Young's trophy case. She is already a high school champion, a 2018 NCAA champion with Notre Dame, a three-time WNBA champion with the Las Vegas Aces and a two-time Olympic gold medalist.

sections.title: Winning in every format
paragraphs: Even those Olympic medals came through two different versions of basketball. Young won 3x3 gold at the Tokyo Games before earning 5x5 gold in Paris. Now she can add World Cup champion.

This was not simply a medal added from the end of the bench. Young became one of Team USA's stabilizers when France threatened to take the final away. While the moment grew heavier, Young stayed steady.

Different uniforms. Different teammates. Different kinds of pressure. The result keeps looking familiar. Jackie Young does not just show up where championships happen. Championships have developed a habit of following her.

debates: Where does Jackie Young's championship résumé rank among today's most accomplished players?

posts.title: Four Teams, Two Tickets, No Hiding: The FIBA Final Four Read
posts.imageAlt: Gabby Williams driving for France in an official FIBA World Cup game
posts.dek: The semifinalists rank first through fourth in the live W Score but own only three of 18 top-three stat slots. The Final Four will decide whether France and USA's depth or Germany and Spain's control survives best.

sections.title: The leaderboard paradox
paragraphs: France, USA, Spain and Germany own the four strongest remaining team resumes, yet Final Four players occupy only three of the 18 top-three places across FIBA's six headline statistical categories. Gabby Williams appears twice and Caitlin Clark once. Most of the tournament's loudest individual numbers have already gone home.

That is the Final Four story. France bends the floor with shooting and pressure. USA buries teams beneath lineups. Germany protects the ball and rebounds. Spain trusts Iyana Martin and Awa Fam to create against older, deeper opposition. Team identity, not one dominant scorer, brought all four this far.

sections.title: France wants multiplication; Germany wants preservation
paragraphs: France is shooting 61.4 percent on twos and 45.7 percent from three, while Germany averages only 9.8 turnovers and owns the stronger rebounding average. The favorite wants one mistake to become a run. The host wants every possession to remain its own event.

sections.title: Spain wants a negotiation; USA wants a landslide
paragraphs: USA holds major advantages in fast-break and bench scoring and arrives after a record 108-point quarterfinal. That win also produced 59 first-half points and 31 assists, the first 30-plus assist quarterfinal in World Cup history. Spain's route is to protect the ball, keep the game in the half court and make every empty American possession feel expensive.

debates: Which travels farther in one game: France's shooting or Germany's possession control?
Can Spain keep USA out of transition long enough to turn the semifinal into a closing-time game?
Does a Final Four built by committees change how we should read individual leaderboards?

posts.dek: Three wins do not mean twelve identical performances. Breanna Stewart sets the standard, Chelsea Gray and Aliyah Boston receive credit the box score misses, and Caitlin Clark’s passing cannot completely erase 30.4 percent shooting.

sections.title: The grade measures impact, not just the box score
paragraphs: Team USA finished group play 3 and 0, but a report card should explain how the wins were built, not hand everyone the same gold star. The W Impact Score gives 60 percent of the grade to official FIBA production and 40 percent to role execution, lineup control, defensive responsibility and game context.

That distinction matters. A reserve can shoot efficiently in a narrow assignment without carrying the same burden as a starter who organizes possessions, anchors coverages or absorbs the opponent’s best matchup. This is a three game Team USA snapshot, not a career ranking.

sections.title: Stewart sets the curve, Young owns the closer minutes
paragraphs: Breanna Stewart earns the top grade because she has been USA’s most complete player. Her 18.0 efficiency rating leads the team, her 8.3 rebounds stabilize the interior and her decisions connect both ends of the floor. Paige Bueckers follows with efficient offense, 3.7 assists and 2.6 combined steals and blocks per game.

Jackie Young completes the A tier. She leads USA at 11.3 points per game, is shooting 53.8 percent and delivered the late control that kept Italy from finishing its upset bid. When a game tightened, Young did not blink.

sections.title: Reese, Iriafen and Howard built the pressure layer
paragraphs: Angel Reese has supplied the most consistent interior disruption outside Stewart. Her rebounding, hands and physicality translate whether she scores or not. Kiki Iriafen made a similar impact in only two appearances, while Rhyne Howard gave USA the point of attack defense and deflections needed to speed opponents up.
Their grades reward repeatable tournament skills. Rebounding travels. Ball pressure travels. Defensive possessions that end without a second chance travel.

sections.title: Why Boston and Gray grade above Citron
paragraphs: Aliyah Boston and Chelsea Gray are the clearest examples of why this cannot be a raw efficiency ranking. Boston’s screens, interior positioning and plus 14.7 average margin shape possessions before the box score records anything. Gray organizes spacing, controls tempo and places teammates where their strengths matter.

Sonia Citron has been efficient in her 10.5 minutes per game, but the role is smaller and the responsibility is lighter. Clean execution deserves credit. It does not automatically outweigh the burden carried by Boston and Gray.

sections.title: Clark’s passing keeps her afloat, her shooting pulls her down
paragraphs: Caitlin Clark leads USA with 6.3 assists per game and owns the team’s best average plus minus. Those are real impact markers. So is 30.4 percent shooting, including 25 percent from three.

A 74 is not a dismissal of her playmaking. It reflects the full job. Clark has created quality offense for others, but the missed shots have kept her individual impact below the players delivering on both efficiency and role.

sections.title: What carries into the knockout rounds
paragraphs: USA’s 88.7 team composite score reflects a strong unbeaten start with room to sharpen. The safest formula is Stewart as the two way hub, Young as the pressure release, Bueckers as the connector and the Reese, Iriafen, Howard group keeping the defense active.

The ceiling rises if Clark’s shot normalizes and Gray’s command begins producing cleaner half court offense. Team USA already has enough talent to win. The report card asks which players are making that talent function.

debates: Should lineup control count as heavily as scoring efficiency when grading a tournament team?
How high can Clark’s grade climb if her shooting catches up to her passing in the knockout rounds?

foodSegment.title: Shak’s bite: winning earns respect, not automatic A’s
foodSegment.script: A 3 and 0 record tells us Team USA handled the assignment. It does not tell us every player handled the same assignment. Stewart has been the standard, Young has been the closer, and the next jump depends on turning Clark’s creation and Gray’s control into cleaner half court possessions.

posts.title: One Possession From Overtime: How Two Near Upsets Almost Rewrote the World Cup
posts.imageAlt: Trinity San Antonio walking toward the court in her Puerto Rico uniform at the 2026 FIBA Women's World Cup
posts.dek: Puerto Rico and Italy lost by five combined points. One more make might have changed the bracket, while Trinity San Antonio left behind the tournament's loudest defensive case.

sections.title: Five points from a different bracket
paragraphs: Puerto Rico came within three points of China, while Italy came within two of Australia. Overtime was one clean possession away in both games, but the losses were built before the final shot. China made 57.1 percent of its twos and closed a 66 to 66 game with the decisive run. Italy erased most of a 26 point deficit, yet spent too much energy repairing three quarters of damage.

That makes the what if worth considering. Puerto Rico had the best individual force on the floor in Trinity San Antonio. Italy had all the momentum after a 31 to 13 fourth quarter. Extra time guarantees neither upset, but it could have changed the emotional and tactical terms of both games.

sections.title: San Antonio's case survives Puerto Rico's exit
paragraphs: San Antonio finished against China with 24 points, 9 rebounds, 7 assists and 5 steals. Her 5.0 steals per game remain the tournament standard. If Puerto Rico had reached overtime and advanced, one more high leverage defensive moment might have made her the clear favorite for Best Defensive Player.

With Puerto Rico out, Gabby Williams carries the strongest active case in the We Know the W Defensive Impact Rating at 96. Angel Reese follows at 92, with Rhyne Howard at 90. San Antonio's elimination changes the runway, not the quality of the résumé.

debates: Should team survival matter more than four games of elite defensive disruption?
Would Puerto Rico or Italy have controlled overtime after owning the late momentum?

posts.title: If We Knew Then What We Know Now: The 2024 WNBA Redraft
posts.dek: Two seasons of WNBA evidence changed the board. Caitlin Clark still goes first, Angel Reese jumps to No. 2, Sydney Taylor rockets from undrafted to No. 6, and the international guards force their way up the first round.

rows: Still the first call. Elite creation, range and playmaking keep the Fever right where they started.
The rebounding, production and night to night impact make her the clearest riser into the top tier.
Size, efficiency and two way value keep the 6 foot 7 center in the exact spot Chicago originally chose her.
A polished scoring forward with three level tools. The talent still looks worthy of the fourth pick.
Her growth as a creator pushes her four spots higher and gives Dallas a different answer at guard.
The class's biggest draft night reversal. An undrafted guard has played her way into the middle of Round 1.
Defensive pressure, pace and playmaking move the French guard into the top seven.
The ceiling is still enormous, but a redraft has to weigh availability and the WNBA sample we have actually seen.
Reliable frontcourt production keeps her safely in Round 1, even as several guards jump past her.
Still a first round guard, but the class has produced more high impact risers than draft night projected.
The second round pick earns a first round seat in the redo after proving she belongs in a WNBA rotation.
The upside and development case keep Atlanta's original final first round slot intact.

sections.title: The top stays Caitlin, but No. 2 changed everything
paragraphs: Caitlin Clark is the easy part of this exercise. Indiana had the first pick in 2024 and still makes the same call. The harder question starts immediately after her, because Angel Reese has erased the idea that seventh was the right place for her to wait.

Reese moves all the way to No. 2 in this redraft. Her rebounding has become a nightly game plan problem, her offensive responsibility has grown, and her impact is too large to leave outside the first two picks. That move alone reshapes the entire board.

sections.title: Cardoso and Jackson are the rare draft night holds
paragraphs: Kamilla Cardoso stays third and Rickea Jackson stays fourth. That is not a lack of movement, it is a compliment to how well those original selections have aged. Cardoso gives Chicago a massive interior presence with two way value. Jackson has shown the scoring package and positional versatility that made her one of the safest offensive prospects in the class.
In a redraft full of risers and slides, holding your original top four position is its own receipt.

sections.title: The middle of the round belongs to the risers
paragraphs: Carla Leite climbs from ninth to fifth, Sydney Taylor goes from undrafted to sixth, and Leila Lacan moves from tenth to seventh. That is the section of the board that looks most different with hindsight.

Leite and Lacan give this class two international guards whose WNBA translation looks stronger now than it did on draft night. Taylor is the loudest story of all. She was not one of the 36 names called in 2024. In this version, Washington takes her sixth. Draft night said undrafted. The floor said first round.

sections.title: Brink at eight is not a talent verdict
paragraphs: Cameron Brink dropping from second to eighth will be the pick people argue about most. The defensive ceiling is still obvious, and healthy Brink can change a game without needing touches. But a redraft based on what players have shown in the WNBA has to count availability and sample size alongside upside.
That makes eighth a statement about the evidence available today, not a claim that seven players have a higher long term ceiling.

sections.title: Round 1 has two new names
paragraphs: Aaliyah Edwards and Jacy Sheldon remain in the first round, but both slide as the risers pass them. Isobel Borlase makes one of the quieter jumps, moving from pick 20 into the No. 11 slot. Nyadiew Puoch stays at 12, preserving Atlanta's original selection.

The two original first rounders who fall out are Alissa Pili, originally eighth, and Marquesha Davis, originally eleventh. That does not erase what got them drafted. It shows how quickly a class can reorder itself once projection turns into professional evidence.

sections.title: Shak's takeaway: draft night is the opening sentence
paragraphs: The fun of a redraft is not pretending front offices should have known the future. It is seeing which skills translated, which opportunities changed careers, and which players forced the league to reconsider the label attached to them.

The 2024 class now has a No. 1 who still looks like No. 1, a No. 7 who looks like No. 2, and an undrafted player who looks like a lottery level selection. That is why the draft matters, but development, health, fit and opportunity get the last word.

sections.title: One important note about the team logos
paragraphs: The teams on this redraft board follow the original 2024 first round draft order. They are not the players' current teams. The question is simple: if each franchise could make its 2024 selection again with what we know now, who would it take?

debates: Does Angel Reese have the strongest case for the biggest rise in the 2024 class?
How high would a fully healthy Cameron Brink go if the redraft were based on ceiling instead of WNBA evidence to date?
Is Sydney Taylor the best undrafted success story from this class?
Which international guard would you take first today, Carla Leite or Leila Lacan?

foodSegment.title: Draft Night Is a Receipt, Not a Life Sentence
foodSegment.script: Caitlin still goes one. Angel refuses to wait until seven. Carla and Leila move up the line, and Sydney Taylor walks into the first round without ever hearing her name called on draft night. That is the whole point of the redo. Scouts draft projections. The league grades translation. Two years later, this class has handed us a very different receipt.

posts.title: Four Months, Four Receipts: Is the Rookie of the Year Race Already Olivia Miles’ ?
posts.dek: Olivia Miles has won every Kia Rookie of the Month award available this season. That makes her the clear leader, but Flau'jae Johnson, Sydney Taylor, Azzi Fudd and Kiki Rice still tell us something important about how deep this rookie class really is.

rows: 19.7 PPG, 4.6 RPG, 6.0 APG through 38 games, plus all four Kia Rookie of the Month awards.
14.1 PPG, 4.8 RPG, 2.9 APG with two way impact, plus the No. 1 W Score on the latest We Know the W Rookie of the Week board.
14.7 PPG as an undrafted rookie, one of the best pure scoring stories in the class.
13.1 PPG and 1.7 steals per game before a right knee procedure ended her rookie season.
11.2 PPG, 4.0 RPG and 2.8 APG while carrying real creation responsibility for an expansion team.

sections.title: Four months is a pattern, not a hot streak
paragraphs: There is a point in every award race when we have to stop asking who is ahead and start asking what someone else would have to do to catch them. Olivia Miles has reached that point. May belonged to Miles. June belonged to Miles. July belonged to Miles. August belonged to Miles. Four months in the league, four Kia Rookie of the Month awards.

The August receipt might be the loudest one yet. Miles averaged 20.6 points, 4.3 rebounds and 6.5 assists for the month. That is not rookie production being graded on a curve. That is lead guard production on a team trying to win the whole thing.

sections.title: The strongest challenger is making the weekly argument
paragraphs: Flau'jae Johnson has not matched Miles month for month, but she keeps building the kind of case that survives beyond one statistic. She scores, rebounds, defends and has taken on important possessions for Seattle without looking like the moment is too big.

The latest We Know the W Rookie of the Week board is a perfect example. Johnson finished Week 14 at No. 1 with a 29.1 W Score after averaging 19.5 points, 3.0 rebounds and 2.0 assists across two games. A weekly board does not decide Rookie of the Year, but it shows who is applying pressure right now.

sections.title: Sydney Taylor is the reminder that draft night is not destiny
paragraphs: Sydney Taylor was not drafted. She also entered September averaging 14.7 points per game. Those two sentences belong next to each other because they explain why this rookie class deserves more attention than one trophy race can hold.

Taylor's Rookie of the Year path is harder because Miles has the stronger all around case and a full season of monthly hardware, but Taylor has already turned an undrafted label into a footnote. That is a different kind of rookie victory.

sections.title: Azzi Fudd's season ended, her impact did not
paragraphs: The No. 1 pick was still firmly in the rookie conversation before right knee soreness led to a season ending arthroscopic procedure. Fudd finished her year at 13.1 points, 1.7 rebounds, 1.8 assists and 1.7 steals per game, while shooting 39.7 percent from three.

Availability matters in an award race, especially against a player producing at Miles' level across a longer season. Still, Fudd's rookie year gave Dallas shooting, point of attack defense and a historic All Star weekend moment when she became the first rookie to win the WNBA three point contest.

sections.title: Kiki Rice has the expansion tax
paragraphs: Kiki Rice's numbers do not jump off the page the way Miles' do, but context matters. Toronto is building a team and an identity at the same time, and Rice has been asked to create inside that uncertainty. An 11 point scoring average with rebounding and playmaking responsibility is a strong foundation for a first year guard.

The Rookie of the Year ballot is not a projection award, so upside alone cannot move Rice ahead of Miles today. But if we are asking which rookies look like long term franchise pieces, Rice belongs in the conversation.

sections.title: So, is there still a race?
paragraphs: Technically, yes. Basketball still has games left, and awards should not be handed out before the schedule is finished. Practically, Olivia Miles has built a gap that now requires an extraordinary closing argument from everyone behind her and a real decline from Miles herself.

The better question might be what kind of Rookie of the Year season we are watching. Miles is not simply leading rookies in a weak class. She is putting up nearly 20 points and six assists a night for Minnesota while sweeping the league's monthly rookie awards. That makes this less about whether she belongs at the top and more about how high her rookie season will eventually sit in WNBA history.

sections.title: What I am watching next
paragraphs: The weekly archive matters now because it can show us whether the gap is tightening before a season average catches up. If Johnson keeps stacking No. 1 weekly W Scores, if Taylor keeps scoring at this level and if Rice closes with a bigger creation load, the race gets more interesting even if the favorite does not change.
For now, the ballot starts with Olivia Miles. The rest of the rookie class is not disappearing behind her. It is giving us several different versions of what a successful first season can look like.

posts.dek: Golden State showed the pressure version. Atlanta showed the possession version. With Courtney Williams back and Minnesota still losing, the Lynx blueprint is getting harder to dismiss.

paragraphs: The Dream beat Minnesota 89 to 81 with Courtney Williams back in the Lynx lineup, shrinking the biggest asterisk attached to the earlier Golden State loss.
Atlanta did not copy Golden State. The Dream won the glass, hit 13 threes, moved the ball through multiple creators and showed there is more than one way to make Minnesota uncomfortable.

Atlanta, Dallas, Los Angeles and Seattle each rank two places higher than their official standing. Las Vegas, Indiana, Washington and Connecticut land in exactly the same position on both lists.

posts.title: The Dream Beat the Lynx. Now Minnesota Has a Pattern Problem.
posts.dek: Atlanta beat Minnesota 89 to 81, won the season series 2 to 1 and handed the Lynx a second straight loss. The methods were different from Golden State, but the pressure points are starting to look repeatable.

sections.title: A different version of the blueprint
paragraphs: Atlanta did not need to win the turnover battle. The Dream made 13 threes to Minnesota's six, outrebounded the Lynx 37 to 32 and built a 52 to 41 halftime lead.

Allisha Gray finished with 23 points and 11 rebounds, Jordin Canada had 16 points and 10 assists, and Angel Reese recorded 15 points and 11 rebounds for a WNBA record 29th double double of the season. Olivia Miles scored 21 for Minnesota but finished with zero assists.

posts.title: Kelsey Mitchell Is the WNBA's First 1,000 Point Guard
posts.dek: Mitchell's 34 against Connecticut pushed her to 1,001 points, making her the first guard and only the second player ever to score 1,000 in one WNBA season.

sections.title: The line moved
paragraphs: A'ja Wilson created the 1,000 point season club. Kelsey Mitchell just became its first guard, reaching the mark with elite efficiency and a season that is still moving.

posts.title: A’ja Wilson's Name Is Written Into South Carolina's Nike Deal
posts.dek: South Carolina's 10 year Nike agreement formally prices A’ja Wilson signature shoes and Wilson related marketing into the benefits promised to the university.

sections.title: Boardroom leverage, with receipts
paragraphs: The public record does not prove Wilson singlehandedly caused the Nike deal. It does show something unusually concrete: her signature product and marketing connection carry explicit contractual value inside a university wide agreement covering all 21 Gamecocks programs.

posts.title: Rickea Jackson Is Officially Aboard for Season 3

sections.title: The official board changed the status
paragraphs: The newer official roster reveal supersedes the earlier availability report. Jackson is now on the active Season 3 board, and the outdated out for 2027 label has been removed.
